issues.subcategory: simulated data presented as real results
issues.description: The abstract, method, and results sections explicitly state they were written using a randomized/dummy dataset generated by Qualtrics to simulate what results will look like after data collection. This means all reported statistics, means, standard deviations, p-values, and effect sizes in the results section are fabricated and do not reflect actual empirical findings. Publishing or submitting a manuscript with simulated results presented in the same format as real results is deeply misleading, even with the disclaimer. Readers may not notice the disclaimer, and the abstract does not sufficiently caveat that all numbers are fictional.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The original studies used between-subjects designs where participants were randomly assigned to conditions. The replication embeds both studies into a single experiment described as a 'within-subject design.' This is a fundamental design change that introduces demand characteristics, order effects, and carryover effects. Participants who see multiple victim conditions (identifiable, statistical, joint) will likely recognize the manipulation and adjust their responses accordingly, completely undermining the ecological validity of the identifiable victim effect manipulation. This change is not adequately justified and is likely to produce null or distorted results.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.description: The procedure states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.' This means participants were not randomly assigned to conditions but self-selected into them. This completely eliminates the experimental control necessary to make causal inferences about the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation. Self-selection introduces massive confounds: participants who choose to learn about the identifiable victim effect may differ systematically from those who do not. This invalidates any causal interpretation of the results.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The original study used real monetary donations—participants received $5 from a prior survey and donated actual money. The replication uses imaginary/hypothetical donations ('Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5'). Research consistently shows that hypothetical and real monetary decisions differ substantially, with hypothetical donations typically being inflated and less sensitive to experimental manipulations. This change fundamentally alters the dependent variable and undermines the validity of the replication.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: All statistical results reported—including F-values, t-values, p-values, means, standard deviations, effect sizes, and confidence intervals—are derived from a randomly generated dataset, not from actual participant responses. Drawing any conclusions from these statistics is invalid. The manuscript nonetheless interprets these results as if they were real findings, stating conclusions such as 'no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect' and 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation.' These conclusions are entirely unfounded.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.description: Several links in the manuscript are placeholder text ('enter link here') indicating the manuscript was submitted or shared before key materials were finalized. This prevents verification of the pre-registration and other materials, undermining the open-science claims of the paper.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: merging two separate studies without justification
issues.description: Studies 1 and 3 of the original article were designed as separate experiments with different manipulations and purposes. Merging them into a single study changes the experimental logic of both. Study 1 tested explicit debiasing; Study 3 tested implicit debiasing through joint presentation. Combining them means participants may be exposed to both manipulations, creating interference effects. The authors acknowledge this but do not adequately address the methodological consequences.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.description: The results state that 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' This is the opposite direction from the identifiable victim effect, which predicts higher donations to identifiable victims. While this could be a genuine null or reversed finding, it is presented without adequate discussion of whether this reversal is meaningful or an artifact of the simulated data and flawed design.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.subcategory: effect sizes extremely small despite statistical significance
issues.description: The reported effect sizes are extremely small (ηp2 = .007 for identifiability, .001 for intervention, .008 for interaction) compared to the original study (ηp2 = .06, .04, .04). With N=1000, the study has very high power to detect trivially small effects. The statistically significant results for identifiability and interaction are likely Type I errors or artifacts of the large sample size rather than meaningful replications of the original effects. The manuscript does not adequately address this discrepancy in effect size magnitude.
issues.quote: Identifiability... Replication | 2 | 3.58 | .028* | .007 | [0.00, 0.02]

issues.subcategory: confidence intervals for effect sizes include zero
issues.description: All reported confidence intervals for effect sizes (ηp2) include zero (e.g., [0.00, 0.02]), indicating that the true effect size could plausibly be zero. Despite this, the manuscript treats statistically significant results as supporting the hypotheses. This is a misinterpretation of statistical significance when confidence intervals span zero.

issues.subcategory: online MTurk sample vs. laboratory student sample
issues.description: The original study recruited participants in a university student center in Pennsylvania, providing a controlled laboratory environment with real monetary stakes. The replication uses Amazon Mechanical Turk workers completing an online survey. MTurk samples differ from student samples in age, motivation, attention, and familiarity with psychological research paradigms. The average age of the simulated sample (M=67.80) is implausibly high for an MTurk sample and suggests the random data generation was not constrained to realistic parameters.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males)

issues.description: The simulated sample has a mean age of 67.80 (SD=30.10) with an age range of 18-120. A mean age of nearly 68 with a standard deviation of 30 and maximum of 120 is statistically and practically impossible for any real human sample. This reveals that the random data generation was entirely unconstrained and bears no resemblance to what actual data would look like, further undermining any interpretation of the simulated results.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10... Age range (years) | Not specified | 18-120 | 18-120

issues.description: The post-hoc test for perceived impact of donation finds that statistical victim condition (M=3.12) has higher perceived impact than the joint condition (M=2.85), but the hypothesis (H6) predicted that identifiable victims would elicit higher perceived impact than statistical victims. The significant finding is between statistical and joint conditions, not between identifiable and statistical as hypothesized. The manuscript's conclusion that 'Results have supported the hypothesis' is therefore incorrect.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34)

issues.description: The abstract states 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.' However, the actual post-hoc results show the significant difference is between statistical victims and the joint condition, not between identifiable and statistical victims as the abstract implies. The identifiable vs. statistical comparison was not significant (p=1.000 after Bonferroni correction).
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The manuscript conducts numerous statistical tests across multiple dependent variables (donation, aggregated feelings, five segregated feelings, perceived impact, correlations across six conditions) without a comprehensive correction for familywise error rate. While Bonferroni correction is applied within some post-hoc tests, the overall Type I error rate across all tests is not controlled. With this many tests, some significant results are expected by chance alone.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions

issues.subcategory: ordered probit regression dropped without justification
issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression as a primary analysis method. The replication explicitly states 'This test would not be conducted in the replication' without providing adequate statistical justification. The donation variable (0-5 dollars in integer increments) is ordinal, making probit regression more appropriate than ANOVA. Dropping this analysis changes the statistical approach in a way that may affect results and reduces comparability with the original.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: table formatting errors and redundant statistics
issues.description: In Table 1, the F-statistic, p-value, and ηp2 for identifiability are repeated identically for both 'Identifiable victim' and 'Statistical victim' rows, which are subgroups of the identifiability factor. These subgroups should not have their own F-statistics; only the overall factor should. This suggests a misunderstanding of how ANOVA results are reported.

issues.subcategory: missing standard deviations in original study summary
issues.description: Table 2 reports means for Study 3 conditions but lists all standard deviations as N/A. While this may reflect incomplete reporting in the original article, the replication authors should have attempted to obtain these values from the authors or noted this as a limitation for the power analysis, as effect size calculations without SDs require assumptions that should be made explicit.
issues.quote: Identifiable victim | 2.38 | N/A | 2 | N/A | 5.67 | <.01** | .07

issues.description: The introduction reports effect sizes from the original study as Cohen's d (e.g., d = 0.48), but the power analysis was apparently conducted using these d values. However, the replication reports results using ηp2. These are different metrics and the conversion between them depends on the design. The manuscript does not clearly explain how d values were derived from the original ANOVA results or how they were used in power analysis, making the power analysis difficult to evaluate.
issues.quote: The effect size of the identifiable victim effect was not reported in the original study. Further calculation of the effect size and confidence interval was included in the supplementary... In Study 1, the main effect of identifiability on donation was d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84]

issues.subcategory: updated victim stimuli changes ecological validity
issues.description: The replication uses updated victim information from Save the Children's website rather than the original stimuli. While the authors justify this as necessary because the original stimuli are dated, changing the specific victim described (name, age, story, photo) changes the stimulus in ways that could substantially affect emotional responses and donation behavior. The identifiable victim effect is sensitive to the specific characteristics of the victim presented.
issues.quote: Updated victim information: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.description: In the original study, participants earned $5 from a prior survey and donated from this money, creating real financial stakes. The replication removes this element entirely. The absence of prior earnings means participants have no real endowment to donate from, which changes the psychological framing of the donation decision. Donating from money you have just earned differs from indicating a hypothetical amount.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey: Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: extension variable added to feeling scale without validation
issues.description: The 'perceived impact of donation' is added as an extension to the feeling variables scale without reporting any validation of this measure, its psychometric properties, or how it was operationalized. The manuscript does not report the specific question wording, scale anchors, or reliability of this measure. Adding an unvalidated measure to an existing scale and then conducting inferential statistics on it is methodologically problematic.
issues.quote: Perceived impact (Extension) | 2 | 3.11 | .006 | [0.00,0.02] | .045*

issues.subcategory: power analysis not reported in main text
issues.description: The power analysis is repeatedly referenced but relegated entirely to supplementary materials. For a pre-registered replication study where sample size justification is critical, the power analysis should be reported in the main text. The manuscript only states the sample size was 'determined to ensure adequate statistical power' without specifying the target power level, assumed effect size, or resulting required N.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.description: The manuscript contains numerous typographical errors, grammatical mistakes, and awkward phrasing throughout, including 'asserts' instead of 'assets,' 'Solvic' instead of 'Slovic' (repeated multiple times), 'fill up' instead of 'complete,' 'Hypothese' instead of 'Hypotheses,' and 'close to very close replication' used inconsistently. These errors suggest insufficient proofreading and reduce the manuscript's credibility.
issues.quote: the lack of efficiency in resource allocation when asserts are accumulated on a single victim... Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks... Hypothese 3 and 4

issues.subcategory: student ID number included in public document
issues.description: The manuscript includes a student ID number (3035682015) in a table of author details. Publishing a student's ID number in a public document raises privacy and data protection concerns and should be removed.
issues.quote: Yik Chun | Wong | ... | 3035682015

issues.subcategory: correlation results not compared to original adequately
issues.description: The original study found a significant correlation between aggregated feelings and donation for the identifiable/no intervention condition (r=.55, p<.01). The replication found r=.02 (p=.803) for the same condition. This is a dramatic discrepancy that warrants substantial discussion. The manuscript dismisses this with a single sentence without exploring why the correlations are near-zero across all conditions, which may reflect the use of random data rather than any real psychological phenomenon.
issues.quote: Results shown in Table 15 suggested that no significant correlation was found across all conditions which is contrary to the original study that aggregated feelings correlated strongly with donation when participants faced an identifiable victim without knowing the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: availability heuristic misattributed as explanation for identifiable victim effect
issues.description: The introduction attributes the identifiable victim effect partly to the 'availability heuristic,' citing Tversky and Kahneman (1973). However, the availability heuristic refers to judging frequency or probability based on ease of recall, not to affective responses to identifiable individuals. The mechanism described (stronger affective reactions to personalized individuals) is more accurately described as the affect heuristic or identifiability per se, not availability. This reflects a conceptual misunderstanding.
issues.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.description: The manuscript has no discussion section. After the results tables, the manuscript moves directly to references. A discussion section is essential for interpreting findings, comparing them to the original study, addressing limitations, and drawing conclusions. Its complete absence is a major structural deficiency.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation. Results shown in Table 15 suggested that no significant correlation was found across all conditions... References

issues.description: The manuscript references Figure 3 (violin plot for identifiability on donation) and Figure 4 (violin plot for intervention on donation) but these figures are not included in the manuscript. This makes it impossible to evaluate the distributional properties of the data.
issues.quote: Figure 3. A violin plot with jittered data for the main effect of identifiability on donation... Figure 4. A violin plot with jittered data for the main effect of intervention on donation.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly cites 'Solvic (2007)' (misspelled) in the introduction when referring to Slovic (2007). Additionally, the reference list contains two different Slovic (2007) entries: one for the genocide paper and one for the affect heuristic paper (with different co-authors). The in-text citations do not distinguish between these two papers, creating ambiguity about which paper is being cited.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon... Solvic (2007) urged the public not to rely on our unreliable emotional responses

issues.description: The manuscript states 'Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period' but does not specify when pre-registration was completed relative to data collection. For a pre-registered study, it is essential to confirm that the pre-registration was completed before any data collection began. The statement is ambiguous and could imply data collection started simultaneously with or before pre-registration.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period. Power analyses and all materials used in these experiments are available in the supplementary materials.

issues.subcategory: exclusion criteria applied to simulated data
issues.description: The manuscript states that participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those who failed attention checks were excluded. However, since the data is randomly generated by Qualtrics, these exclusion criteria could not have been meaningfully applied. The reported N=1000 after exclusions is therefore not a realistic estimate of the final sample size, and the exclusion process cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The post-hoc test for identifiable vs. statistical victim condition on donation yields pBonferroni=.049, which is barely significant after correction. Given that this result is based on simulated random data and the effect size is trivially small (d=0.076), this borderline significant result is likely a Type I error and should not be interpreted as supporting the identifiable victim effect.

The manuscript cites Lee and Feeley's (2016) meta-analysis finding an overall mean effect size of only 0.05 but then states 'the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial.' An effect size of d=0.05 is negligible by any standard interpretation. The authors do not grapple with the implication that the identifiable victim effect may be much smaller than assumed, which is directly relevant to the power analysis and interpretation of the replication.
issues.quote: Although the overall mean effect size was only 0.05, the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial to encourage altruistic behaviour towards the needy

issues.description: The CRediT table lists 'So Chi Liu' as contributing to pre-registration peer review and data analysis peer review, but this person does not appear in the author list. It is unclear whether this person should be an author or acknowledged contributor, and their institutional affiliation and role in the project are not described.
issues.quote: Pre-registration peer review / verification | | | X Data analysis peer review/verification | | | X

issues.subcategory: word count placeholders not filled in
issues.description: The manuscript header shows 'Word: abstract – [136], manuscript - [7394]' with bracketed numbers suggesting these are placeholder values that were not properly formatted or verified. This is a minor but indicative sign of incomplete manuscript preparation.
issues.quote: Word: abstract – [136], manuscript - [7394]

issues.subcategory: intervention applied to joint condition without original precedent
issues.description: The replication applies the explicit intervention (learning about the identifiable victim effect) to the joint condition, which was not done in the original study. This creates a new experimental cell that has no direct comparison in the original study, making it impossible to evaluate whether this condition replicates anything from the original. The authors acknowledge this as a deviation but do not adequately discuss how it affects the interpretation of results.
issues.quote: Intervention applied to the joint condition: To combine study 1 and 3 into a single study, intervention will be applied to the joint condition to allow the comparison of explicit and implicit manipulation with fewer confounds.
